=The structure of main verb (selbri)=
==Lojban content words: brivla==
At the center, logically and often physically, of every Lojban bridi is one or more words which constitute the selbri. A bridi expresses a relationship between things: the selbri specifies which relationship is referred to. The difference between:

:'''do mamta mi'''
:<code>You are-a-mother-of me</code>
:''You are my mother''

and

:'''do patfu mi'''
:<code>You are-a-father-of me.</code>
:''You are my father.''

lies in the different selbri.

The simplest kind of selbri is a single Lojban content word: a brivla. There are three different varieties of brivla: those which are built into the language (the gismu), those which are derived from combinations of the gismu (the lujvo), and those which are taken (usually in a modified form) from other languages (the fu'ivla). In addition, there are a few cmavo that can act like brivla; these are mentioned in {{ls|section-cmavo-selbri}}, and discussed in full in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}.

For the purposes of this chapter, however, all brivla are alike. For example,

:'''ta bloti'''
:<code>That is-a-boat.</code>
:''That is a boat.''

:'''ta brablo'''
:<code>That is-a-large-boat.</code>
:''That is a ship.''

:'''ta blotrskunri'''
:<code>That is-a-(boat)-schooner.</code>
:''That is a schooner.''

illustrate the three types of brivla (gismu, lujvo, and fu'ivla respectively), but in each case the selbri is composed of a single word whose meaning can be learned independent of its origins.

The remainder of this chapter will mostly use gismu as example brivla, because they are short. However, it is important to keep in mind that wherever a gismu appears, it could be replaced by any other kind of brivla.

{{ssp|section-simple-tanru}}
==Simple tanru==

Beyond the single brivla, a selbri may consist of two brivla placed together. When a selbri is built in this way from more than one brivla, it is called a tanru, a word with no single English equivalent. The nearest analogue to tanru in English are combinations of two nouns such as “lemon tree”. There is no way to tell just by looking at the phrase “lemon tree” exactly what it refers to, even if you know the meanings of “lemon” and “tree” by themselves. As English-speakers, we must simply know that it refers to “a tree which bears lemons as fruits”. A person who didn't know English very well might think of it as analogous to “brown tree” and wonder, “What kind of tree is lemon-colored?”

In Lojban, tanru are also used for the same purposes as English adjective-noun combinations like “big boy” and adverb-verb combinations like “quickly run”. This is a consequence of Lojban not having any such categories as “noun”, “verb”, “adjective”, or “adverb”. English words belonging to any of these categories are translated by simple brivla in Lojban. Here are some examples of tanru:

:'''tu pelnimre tricu'''
:<code>That-yonder is-a-(lemon tree).</code>
:''That is a lemon tree.''

:'''la djan. barda nanla'''
:<code>That-named John is-a-big boy.</code>
:''John is a big boy.''

:'''mi sutra bajra'''
:<code>I quick run</code>
:''I quickly run./I run quickly.''

Note that {{vla|pelnimre}} is a lujvo for “lemon”; it is derived from the gismu {{vla|pelxu}}, yellow, and {{vla|nimre}}, citrus. Note also that {{vla|sutra}} can mean “fast/quick” or “quickly” depending on its use:

:'''mi sutra'''
:<code>I am-fast/quick</code>

shows {{vla|sutra}} used to translate an adjective, whereas in {{lex|example-random-id-eD63}} it is translating an adverb. (Another correct translation of {{lex|example-random-id-eD63}}, however, would be “I am a quick runner”.)

There are special Lojban terms for the two components of a tanru, derived from the place structure of the word {{vla|tanru}}. The first component is called the {{vla|seltau}}, and the second component is called the {{vla|tertau}}.

The most important rule for use in interpreting tanru is that the tertau carries the primary meaning. A 
:{{jbo|pelnimre tricu}} is primarily a tree, and only secondarily is it connected with lemons in some way. For this reason, an alternative translation of {{lex|example-lemon-tree}} would be:

That is a lemon type of tree.

This “type of” relationship between the components of a tanru is fundamental to the tanru concept.

We may also say that the seltau modifies the meaning of the tertau:

That is a tree which is lemon-ish (in the way appropriate to trees)

would be another possible translation of {{lex|example-lemon-tree}}. In the same way, a more explicit translation of {{lex|example-random-id-qHNA}} might be:

John is a boy who is big in the way that boys are big.

This “way that boys are big” would be quite different from the way in which elephants are big; big-for-a-boy is small-for-an-elephant.

All tanru are ambiguous semantically. Possible translations of:

:'''ta klama jubme'''
:<code>That is-a-goer type-of-table.</code>

include:
*  That is a table which goes (a wheeled table, perhaps).
*That is a table owned by one who goes.
*That is a table used by those who go (a sports doctor's table?).
*That is a table when it goes (otherwise it is a chair?).

In each case the object referred to is a “goer type of table”, but the ambiguous “type of” relationship can mean one of many things. A speaker who uses tanru (and pragmatically all speakers must) takes the risk of being misunderstood. Using tanru is convenient because they are short and expressive; the circumlocution required to squeeze out all ambiguity can require too much effort.

No general theory covering the meaning of all possible tanru exists; probably no such theory can exist. However, some regularities obviously do exist:

:'''do barda prenu'''
:<code>You are-a-large person.</code>

:'''do cmalu prenu'''
:<code>You are-a-small person.</code>

are parallel tanru, in the sense that the relationship between {{vla|barda}} and {{vla|prenu}} is the same as that between {{vla|cmalu}} and {{vla|prenu}}. {{ls|section-asymmetric-tanru}} and {{ls|section-symmetric-tanru}} contain a partial listing of some types of tanru, with examples.

{{ssp|section-three-part-tanru}}
==Three-part tanru grouping with {{vla|bo}}==

The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|bo}}
:{{s|BO}}
:''description''

Consider the English sentence:

<!-- FIXME: The indexterm "girls' school" applies to all three of the following examples; should it go in all three or just the first? -->

That's a little girls' school.

What does it mean? Two possible readings are:

That's a little school for girls.

That's a school for little girls.

This ambiguity is quite different from the simple tanru ambiguity described in {{ls|section-simple-tanru}}. We understand that “girls' school” means “a school where girls are the students”, and not “a school where girls are the teachers” or “a school which is a girl” (!). Likewise, we understand that “little girl” means “girl who is small”. This is an ambiguity of grouping. Is “girls' school” to be taken as a unit, with “little” specifying the type of girls' school? Or is “little girl” to be taken as a unit, specifying the type of school? In English speech, different tones of voice, or 
exaggerated speech rhythm showing the grouping, are used to make the distinction; English writing usually leaves it unrepresented.

Lojban makes no use of tones of voice for any purpose; explicit words are used to do the work. The cmavo {{vla|bo}} (which belongs to selma'o BO) may be placed between the two brivla which are most closely associated. Therefore, a Lojban translation of {{lex|example-random-id-5UBW}} would be:

:'''ta cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small girl [] school.</code>{{lex|example-random-id-5UBJ}} might be translated:

:'''ta cmalu bo nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small [] girl school.</code>

The {{vla|bo}} is represented in the literal translation by a hyphen because in written English a hyphen is sometimes used for the same purpose: “a big dog-catcher” would be quite different from a “big-dog catcher” (presumably someone who catches only big dogs).

Analysis of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}} and {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}} reveals a tanru nested within a tanru. In {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, the main tanru has a seltau of {{vla|cmalu}} and a tertau of 
:{{jbo|nixli bo ckule}}; the tertau is itself a tanru with {{vla|nixli}} as the seltau and {{vla|ckule}} as the tertau. In {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}, on the other hand, the seltau is 
:{{jbo|cmalu bo nixli}} (itself a tanru), whereas the tertau is {{vla|ckule}}. 
This structure of tanru nested within tanru forms the basis for all the more complex types of selbri that will be explained below.

What about {{lex|example-random-id-9FPm}}? What does it mean?

:'''ta cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small girl school.</code>

The rules of Lojban do not leave this sentence ambiguous, as the rules of English do with {{lex|example-random-id-gCLr}}. The choice made by the language designers is to say that {{lex|example-random-id-9FPm}} means the same as {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}. This is true no matter what three brivla are used: the leftmost two are always grouped together. This rule is called the “left-grouping rule”. Left-grouping in seemingly ambiguous structures is quite common &ndash; though not universal &ndash; in other contexts in Lojban.

Another way to express the English meaning of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}} and {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}, using parentheses to mark grouping, is:

:'''ta cmalu [] nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small type-of (girl type-of school).</code>

:'''ta cmalu bo nixli [] ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(small type-of girl) type-of school.</code>

Because “type-of” is implicit in the Lojban tanru form, it has no Lojban equivalent.

Note: It is perfectly legal, though pointless, to insert {{vla|bo}} into a simple tanru:

:'''ta klama bo jubme'''
:<code>That is-a-goer [] table.</code>

is a legal Lojban bridi that means exactly the same thing as {{lex|example-random-id-aIfM}}, and is ambiguous in exactly the same ways. The cmavo {{vla|bo}} serves only to resolve grouping ambiguity: it says nothing about the more basic ambiguity present in all tanru.

{{ssp|section-complex-grouping}}
==Complex tanru grouping==

If one element of a tanru can be another tanru, why not both elements?

:'''do mutce bo barda gerku bo kavbu'''
:<code>You are-a-(very type-of large) (dog type-of capturer).</code>
:''You are a very large dog-catcher.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-m5SD}}, the selbri is a tanru with seltau 
:{{jbo|mutce bo barda}} and tertau 
:{{jbo|gerku bo kavbu}}. It is worth emphasizing once again that this tanru has the same fundamental ambiguity as all other Lojban tanru: the sense in which the “dog type-of capturer” is said to be “very type-of large” is not precisely specified. Presumably it is his body which is large, but theoretically it could be one of his other properties.

We will now justify the title of this chapter by exploring the ramifications of the phrase “pretty little girls' school”, an expansion of the tanru used in 
{{ls|section-three-part-tanru}} to four brivla. (Although this example has been used in the Loglan Project almost since the beginning &ndash; it first appeared in Quine's book {{cite|book|Word and Object}} (1960) &ndash; it is actually a mediocre example because of the ambiguity of English “pretty”; it can mean “beautiful”, the sense intended here, or it can mean “very”. Lojban {{vla|melbi}} is not subject to this ambiguity: it means only “beautiful”.)

Here are four ways to group this phrase:

:'''ta melbi cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-((pretty type-of little) type-of girl) type-of school.</code>
:''That is a school for girls who are beautifully small.''

:'''ta melbi cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(pretty type-of little) (girl type-of school).</code>
:''That is a girls' school which is beautifully small.''

:'''ta melbi cmalu bo nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(pretty type-of (little type-of girl)) type-of school.</code>
:''That is a school for small girls who are beautiful.''

:'''ta melbi cmalu bo nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of (little type-of (girl type-of school)).</code>
:''That is a small school for girls which is beautiful.''

{{lex|example-random-id-qjop}} uses a construction which has not been seen before: 
:{{jbo|cmalu bo nixli bo ckule}}, with two consecutive uses of {{vla|bo}} between brivla. The rule for multiple {{vla|bo}} constructions is the opposite of the rule when no {{vla|bo}} is present at all: the last two are grouped together. Not surprisingly, this is called the “right-grouping rule”, and it is associated with every use of 
{{vla|bo}} in the language. Therefore,

:'''ta cmalu bo nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-little type-of (girl type-of school).</code>

means the same as {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, not {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}. This rule may seem peculiar at first, but one of its consequences is that {{vla|bo}} is never necessary between the first two elements of any of the complex tanru presented so far: all of {{lex|example-random-id-qjmr}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}} could have {{vla|bo}} inserted between {{vla|melbi}} and {{vla|cmalu}} with no change in meaning.

{{ssp|section-ke-grouping}}
==Complex tanru with {{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}}==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ke}}
:{{s|KE}}
:''description''

:{{c|ke'e}}
:{{s|KEhE}}
:''description''

There is, in fact, a fifth grouping of “pretty little girls' school” that cannot be expressed with the resources explained so far. To handle it, we must introduce the grouping parentheses cmavo, 
{{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}} (belonging to selma'o KE and KEhE respectively). Any portion of a selbri sandwiched between these two cmavo is taken to be a single tanru component, independently of what is adjacent to it. Thus, {{lex|example-random-id-qjmr}} can be rewritten in any of the following ways:

:'''ta ke melbi cmalu ke'e nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-( pretty little ) girl school.</code>

:'''ta ke ke melbi cmalu ke'e nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-( ( pretty little ) girl ) school.</code>

:'''ta ke ke ke melbi cmalu ke'e nixli ke'e ckule ke'e'''
:<code>That is-a-( ( ( pretty little ) girl ) school ).</code>

Even more versions could be created simply by placing any number of {{vla|ke}} cmavo at the beginning of the selbri, and a like number of {{vla|ke'e}} cmavo at its end. Obviously, all of these are a waste of breath once the left-grouping rule has been grasped. However, the following is equivalent to {{lex|example-random-id-qjog}} and may be easier to understand:

:'''ta melbi ke cmalu nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-( pretty type-of ( little type-of girl ) ) type-of school.</code>

Likewise, a {{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}} version of {{lex|example-random-id-qjNi}} would be:

:'''ta melbi cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-(pretty type-of little) ( girl type-of school ).</code>

The final {{vla|ke'e}} is given in square brackets here to indicate that it can be elided. It is always possible to elide 
{{vla|ke'e}} at the end of the selbri, making {{lex|example-random-id-AUdM}} as terse as {{lex|example-random-id-qjNi}}.

Now how about that fifth grouping? It is

:'''ta melbi ke cmalu nixli ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of ( ( little type-of girl ) type-of school ).</code>
:''That is a beautiful school for small girls.''
{{lex|example-random-id-tz0L}} is distinctly different in meaning from any of Examples 4.2 through 4.5. Note that within the {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} parentheses, the left-grouping rule is applied to 
:{{jbo|cmalu nixli ckule}}.

It is perfectly all right to mix {{vla|bo}} and {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} in a single selbri. For instance, {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}}, which in pure {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} form is

:'''ta melbi ke cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e] [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of ( little type-of ( girl type-of school ) ).</code>

can equivalently be expressed as:

:'''ta melbi ke cmalu nixli bo ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of ( little type-of ( girl type-of school ) ).</code>

and in many other different forms as well.

{{ssp|section-logical-connection}}
==Logical connection within tanru==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|je}}
:{{s|JA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ja}}
:{{s|JA}}
:''description''

:{{c|joi}}
:{{s|JOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|gu'e}}
:{{s|GUhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|gi}}
:{{s|GI}}
:''description''

Consider the English phrase “big red dog”. How shall this be rendered as a Lojban tanru? The naive attempt:

:'''barda xunre gerku'''
:<code>(big type-of red) type-of dog</code>

will not do, as it means a dog whose redness is big, in whatever way redness might be described as “big”. Nor is

:'''barda xunre bo gerku'''
:<code>big type-of (red type-of dog)</code>

much better. After all, the straightforward understanding of the English phrase is that the dog is big as compared with other dogs, not merely as compared with other red dogs. In fact, the bigness and redness are independent properties of the dog, and only obscure rules of English adjective ordering prevent us from saying “red big dog”.

The Lojban approach to this problem is to introduce the cmavo {{vla|je}}, which is one of the many equivalents of English “and”. A big red dog is one that is both big and red, and we can say:

:'''barda je xunre gerku'''
:<code>(big and red) type-of dog</code>

Of course,

:'''xunre je barda gerku'''
:<code>(red and big) type-of dog</code>

is equally satisfactory and means the same thing. As these examples indicate, joining two brivla with {{vla|je}} makes them a unit for tanru purposes. However, explicit grouping with {{vla|bo}} or {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} associates brivla more closely than {{vla|je}} does:

:'''barda je pelxu bo xunre gerku'''
:'''barda je ke pelxu xunre ke'e gerku'''
:<code>(big and (yellow type-of red)) dog</code>
:''big yellowish-red dog''

With no grouping indicators, we get:

:'''barda je pelxu xunre gerku'''
:<code>((big and yellow) type-of red) type-of dog</code>
:<code>biggish- and yellowish-red dog</code>

which again raises the question of {{lex|example-random-id-riAq}}: what does “biggish-red” mean?

Unlike {{vla|bo}} and {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}}, {{vla|je}} is useful as well as merely legal within simple tanru. It may be used to partly resolve the ambiguity of simple tanru:

:'''ta blanu je zdani'''
:<code>that is-blue and is-a-house</code>

definitely refers to something which is both blue and is a house, and not to any of the other possible interpretations of simple 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}}. Furthermore, 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}} refers to something which is blue in the way that houses are blue; 
:{{jbo|blanu je zdani}} has no such implication &ndash; the blueness of a 
:{{jbo|blanu je zdani}} is independent of its houseness.

With the addition of {{vla|je}}, many more versions of “pretty little girls' school” are made possible: see 
{{ls|section-pretty-school-groupings}} for a complete list.

A subtle point in the semantics of tanru like {{lex|example-random-id-0UrF}} needs special elucidation. There are at least two possible interpretations of:

:'''ta melbi je nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(beautiful and girl) type-of school.</code>

It can be understood as:

That is a girls' school and a beautiful school.

or as:

That is a school for things which are both girls and beautiful.

The interpretation specified by {{lex|example-random-id-FCDa}} treats the tanru as a sort of abbreviation for:

:'''ta ke melbi ckule ke'e je ke nixli ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-( beautiful type-of school ) and ( girl type-of school )</code>

whereas the interpretation specified by {{lex|example-random-id-aFxm}} does not. This is a kind of semantic ambiguity for which Lojban does not compel a firm resolution. The way in which the school is said to be of type “beautiful and girl” may entail that it is separately a beautiful school and a girls' school; but the alternative interpretation, that the members of the school are beautiful and girls, is also possible. Still another interpretation is:

That is a school for beautiful things and also for girls.

so while the logical connectives help to resolve the meaning of tanru, they by no means compel a single meaning in and of themselves.

In general, logical connectives within tanru cannot undergo the formal manipulations that are possible with the related logical connectives that exist outside tanru; See {{ls|section-tanru}} for further details.

The logical connective {{vla|je}} is only one of the fourteen logical connectives that Lojban provides. Here are a few examples of some of the others:

:'''le bajra cu jinga ja te jinga'''
:''the runner(s) is/are winner(s) or loser(s).''

:'''blanu naja lenku skapi'''
:<code>(blue only-if cold) skin</code>
:''skin which is blue only if it is cold''

:'''xamgu jo tordu nuntavla'''
:<code>(good if-and-only-if short) speech</code>
:''speech which is good if (and only if) it is short''

:'''vajni ju pluka nuntavla'''
:<code>(important whether-or-not pleasing) event-of-talking</code>
:''speech which is important, whether or not it is pleasing''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qJse}}, {{vla|ja}} is grammatically equivalent to {{vla|je}} but means “or” (more precisely, “and/or”). Likewise, {{vla|naja}} means “only if” in {{lex|example-random-id-qJsg}}, {{vla|jo}} means “if and only if” in {{lex|example-random-id-qjsy}}, and {{vla|ju}} means “whether or not” in {{lex|example-random-id-qjtD}}.

Now consider the following example:

:'''ricfu je blanu jabo crino'''
:<code>rich and (blue or green)</code>

which illustrates a new grammatical feature: the use of both {{vla|ja}} and {{vla|bo}} between tanru components. The two cmavo combine to form a compound whose meaning is that of {{vla|ja}} but which groups more closely; {{vla|ja}}{{vla|bo}} is to 
{{vla|ja}} as plain {{vla|bo}} is to no cmavo at all. However, both {{vla|ja}} and {{vla|ja}}{{vla|bo}} group less closely than 
{{vla|bo}} does:

:'''ricfu je blanu jabo crino bo blanu'''
:<code>rich and (blue or green - blue)</code>
:<code>rich and (blue or greenish-blue)</code>

An alternative form of {{lex|example-random-id-NuWM}} is:

:'''ricfu je ke blanu ja crino [ke'e]'''
:<code>rich and (blue or green)</code>

In addition to the logical connectives, there are also a variety of non-logical connectives, grammatically equivalent to the logical ones. The only one with a well-understood meaning in tanru contexts is {{vla|joi}}, which is the kind of “and” that denotes a mixture:

:'''ti blanu joi xunre bolci'''
:<code>This is-a-(blue and red) ball.</code>

The ball described is neither solely red nor solely blue, but probably striped or in some other way exhibiting a combination of the two colors. {{lex|example-random-id-Hr1L}} is distinct from:

:'''ti blanu xunre bolci'''
:''This is a bluish-red ball''

which would be a ball whose color is some sort of purple tending toward red, since {{vla|xunre}} is the more important of the two components. On the other hand,

:'''ti blanu je xunre bolci'''
:<code>This is a (blue and red) ball</code>

is probably self-contradictory, seeming to claim that the ball is independently both blue and red at the same time, although some sensible interpretation may exist.

Finally, just as English “and” has the variant form “both ... and”, so {{vla|je}} between tanru components has the variant form {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}}, where {{vla|gu'e}} is placed before the components and {{vla|gi}} between them:

:'''gu'e barda gi xunre gerku'''
:<code>(both big and red) type-of dog</code>

is equivalent in meaning to {{lex|example-random-id-0UrF}}. For each logical connective related to {{vla|je}}, there is a corresponding connective related to {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} in a systematic way.

The portion of a {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} construction before the {{vla|gi}} is a full selbri, and may use any of the selbri resources including {{vla|je}} logical connections. After the {{vla|gi}}, logical connections are taken to be wider in scope than the {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}}, which has in effect the same scope as {{vla|bo}}:

:'''gu'e barda je xunre gi gerku ja mlatu'''
:<code>(both (big and red) and dog) or cat</code>
:''something which is either big, red, and a dog, or else a cat''

leaves {{vla|mlatu}} outside the {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} construction. The scope of the {{vla|gi}} arm extends only to a single brivla or to two or more brivla connected with {{vla|bo}} or {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}}.

{{ssp|section-be-sumti}}
==Linked sumti: {{vla|be}}-{{vla|bei}}-{{vla|be'o}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|be}}
:{{s|BE}}
:''description''

:{{c|bei}}
:{{s|BEI}}
:''description''

:{{c|be'o}}
:{{s|BEhO}}
:''description''

The question of the place structures of selbri has been glossed over so far. This chapter does not attempt to treat place structure issues in detail; they are discussed in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}}. One grammatical structure related to places belongs here, however. In simple sentences such as {{lex|example-do-mamta-mi}}, the place structure of the selbri is simply the defined place structure of the gismu{{vla|mamta}}. What about more complex selbri?

For tanru, the place structure rule is simple: the place structure of a tanru is always the place structure of its tertau. Thus, the place structure of 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}} is that of {{vla|zdani}}: the x1 place is a house or nest, and the x2 place is its occupants.

What about the places of {{vla|blanu}}? Is there any way to get them into the act? In fact, {{vla|blanu}} has only one place, and this is merged, as it were, with the x1 place of {{vla|zdani}}. It is whatever is in the x1 place that is being characterized as blue-for-a-house. But if we replace {{vla|blanu}} with {{vla|xamgu}}, we get:

:'''ti xamgu zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good house.</code>
:''This is a good (for someone, by some standard) house.''

Since {{vla|xamgu}} has three places (x1, the good thing; x2, the person for whom it is good; and x3, the standard of goodness), {{lex|example-random-id-tffW}} necessarily omits information about the last two: there is no room for them. Room can be made, however!

:'''ti xamgu be do bei mi [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good (for you by-standard me) house.</code>
:''This is a house that is good for you by my standards.''

Here, the gismu {{vla|xamgu}} has been followed by the cmavo {{vla|be}} (of selma'o BE), which signals that one or more sumti follows. These sumti are not part of the overall bridi place structure, but fill the places of the brivla they are attached to, starting with x2. If there is more than one sumti, they are separated by the cmavo {{vla|bei}} (of selma'o BEI), and the list of sumti is terminated by the elidable terminator {{vla|be'o}} (of selma'o BEhO).

Grammatically, a brivla with sumti linked to it in this fashion plays the same role in tanru as a simple brivla. To illustrate, here is a fully fleshed-out version of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, with all places filled in:

:'''ti cmalu be le ka canlu bei lo'e ckule be'o'''
:<code>This is a small (in-dimension the property-of volume by-standard the-typical school)</code>
:'''nixli be li mu bei lo merko be'o bo ckule'''
:<code>(girl (of-years the-number five by-standard some American-thing) school)</code>
:'''la bryklyn. loi pemci'''
:<code>in-Brooklyn with-subject poems</code>
:'''le mela nu,IORK. prenu le jecta'''
:<code>for-audience New-York persons with-operator the state.</code>
This is a school, small in volume compared to the typical school, pertaining to five-year-old girls (by American standards), in Brooklyn, teaching poetry to the New York community and operated by the state.

Here the three places of {{vla|cmalu}}, the three of {{vla|nixli}}, and the four of {{vla|ckule}} are fully specified. Since the places of {{vla|ckule}} are the places of the bridi as a whole, it was not necessary to link the sumti which follow {{vla|ckule}}. It would have been legal to do so, however:

:'''mi klama be le zarci bei le zdani [be'o]'''
:<code>I go (to-the market from-the house).</code>

means the same as

:'''mi klama le zarci le zdani'''
:<code>I go to-the market from-the house.</code>

No matter how complex a tanru gets, the last brivla always dictates the place structure: the place structure of

:'''melbi je cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>a (pretty and little) (girl school)</code>
:''a school for girls which is both beautiful and small''

is simply that of {{vla|ckule}}. (The sole exception to this rule is discussed in {{ls|section-co-inversion}}.)

It is possible to precede linked sumti by the place structure ordering tags 
{{vla|fe}}, {{vla|fi}}, {{vla|fo}}, and {{vla|fu}} (of selma'o FA, discussed further in {{ls|section-FA}}), which serve to explicitly specify the x2, x3, x4, and x5 places respectively. Normally, the place following the {{vla|be}} is the x2 place and the other places follow in order. If it seems convenient to change the order, however, it can be accomplished as follows:

:'''ti xamgu be fi mi bei fe do [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good ( by-standard me for you ) house.</code>

which is equivalent in meaning to {{lex|example-random-id-Uuio}}. Note that the order of {{vla|be}}, {{vla|bei}}, and {{vla|be'o}} does not change; only the inserted {{vla|fi}} tells us that {{vla|mi}} is the x3 place (and correspondingly, the inserted {{vla|fe}} tells us that {{vla|do}} is the x2 place). Changing the order of sumti is often done to match the order of another language, or for emphasis or rhythm.

Of course, using FA cmavo makes it easy to specify one place while omitting a previous place:

:'''ti xamgu be fi mi [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good (by-standard me) house.</code>
:''This is a good house by my standards.''

Similarly, sumti labeled by modal or tense tags can be inserted into strings of linked sumti just as they can into bridi:

:'''ta blanu be ga'a mi [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>That is-a-blue (to-observer me) house.</code>
:''That is a blue, as I see it, house.''

The meaning of {{lex|example-random-id-GstI}} is slightly different from:

:'''ta blanu zdani ga'a mi'''
:<code>That is-a-blue house to-observer me.</code>
:''That is a blue house, as I see it.''

See discussions in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}} of modals and in {{lch|chapter-tenses}} of tenses for more explanations.

The terminator {{vla|be'o}} is almost always elidable: however, if the selbri belongs to a description, then a relative clause following it will attach to the last linked sumti unless 
{{vla|be'o}} is used, in which case it will attach to the outer description:

:'''le xamgu be do noi barda cu zdani'''
:<code>The good-thing for you (who are-large) is-a-house.</code>

:'''le xamgu be do be'o noi barda cu zdani'''
:<code>The (good-thing for you) (which is-large) is-a-house</code>

(Relative clauses are explained in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}.)

In other cases, however, {{vla|be'o}} cannot be elided if {{vla|ku}} has also been elided:

:'''le xamgu be le ctuca [ku] be'o zdani'''
:<code>the good (for the teacher) house</code>

requires either {{vla|ku}} or {{vla|be'o}}, and since there is only one occurrence of {{vla|be}}, the {{vla|be'o}} must match it, whereas it may be confusing which occurrence of {{vla|le}} the {{vla|ku}} terminates (in fact the second one is correct).

{{ssp|section-co-inversion}}
==Inversion of tanru: {{vla|co}}==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|co}}
:{{s|CO}}
:''description''

The standard order of Lojban tanru, whereby the modifier precedes what it modifies, is very natural to English-speakers: we talk of “blue houses”, not of “houses blue”. In other languages, however, such matters are differently arranged, and Lojban supports this reverse order (tertau before seltau) by inserting the particle {{vla|co}}. {{lex|example-random-id-qjtV}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjty}} mean exactly the same thing:

:'''ta blanu zdani'''
:<code>That is-a-blue type-of-house.</code>
:''That is a blue house.''

:'''ta zdani co blanu'''
:<code>That is-a-house of-type blue.</code>
:''That is a blue house.''

This change is called “tanru inversion”. In tanru inversion, the element before 
{{vla|co}} ( {{vla|zdani}} in {{lex|example-random-id-qjty}}) is the tertau, and the element following {{vla|co}} ( {{vla|blanu}}) in {{lex|example-random-id-qjty}}) is the seltau.

The meaning, and more specifically, the place structure, of a tanru is not affected by inversion: the place structure of 
:{{jbo|zdani co blanu}} is still that of {{vla|zdani}}. However, the existence of inversion in a selbri has a very special effect on any sumti which follow that selbri. Instead of being interpreted as filling places of the selbri, they actually fill the places (starting with x2) of the seltau. In {{ls|section-be-sumti}}, we saw how to fill interior places with {{vla|be}}&hellip;{{vla|bei}}&hellip;{{vla|be'o}}, and in fact {{lex|example-random-id-qjuc}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}} have the same meaning:

:'''mi klama be le zarci bei le zdani be'o troci'''
:<code>I am-a-(goer to the market from the house) type-of trier.</code>
:''I try to go to the market from the house.''

:'''mi troci co klama le zarci le zdani'''
:<code>I am-a-trier of-type (goer to-the market from-the house).</code>
:''I try to go to the market from the house.''
{{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}} is a less deeply nested construction, requiring fewer cmavo. As a result it is probably easier to understand.

Note that in Lojban “trying to go” is expressed using {{vla|troci}} as the tertau. The reason is that “trying to go” is a “going type of trying”, not a “trying type of going”. The trying is more fundamental than the going &ndash; if the trying fails, we may not have a going at all.

Any sumti which precede a selbri with an inverted tanru fill the places of the selbri (i.e., the places of the tertau) in the ordinary way. In {{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}}, {{vla|mi}} fills the x1 place of 
:{{jbo|troci co klama}}, which is the x1 place of {{vla|troci}}. The other places of the selbri remain unfilled. The trailing sumti 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} and 
:{{jbo|le zdani}} do not occupy selbri places, despite appearances.

As a result, the regular mechanisms (involving selma'o VOhA and GOhI, explained in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}) for referring to individual sumti of a bridi cannot refer to any of the trailing places of {{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}}, because they are not really “sumti of the bridi” at all.

When inverting a more complex tanru, it is possible to invert it only at the most general modifier-modified pair. The only possible inversion of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, for instance, is:

:'''ta nixli [bo] ckule co cmalu'''
:<code>That (is-a-girl type-of school) of-type little.</code>
:''That's a girls' school which is small.''

Note that the {{vla|bo}} of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}} is optional in {{lex|example-random-id-7uS2}}, because {{vla|co}} groups more loosely than any other cmavo used in tanru, including none at all. Not even {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} parentheses can encompass a {{vla|co}}:

:'''ta cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e] co melbi'''
:<code>That is-a-(little type-of (girl type-of school)) of-type pretty.</code>
:''That's a small school for girls which is beautiful.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-y501}}, the {{vla|ke'e}} is automatically inserted before the {{vla|co}} rather than at its usual place at the end of the selbri. As a result, there is a simple and mechanical rule for removing {{vla|co}} from any selbri: change “A co B” to “ke B ke'e A”. (At the same time, any sumti following the selbri must be transformed into {{vla|be}}&hellip;{{vla|bei}}&hellip;{{vla|be'o}} form and attached following B.) Therefore,

:'''ckule co melbi nixli'''
:<code>school of-type pretty girl</code>
:''school for beautiful girls''

means the same as:

:'''ke melbi nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>(pretty girl) school</code>

Multiple {{vla|co}} cmavo can appear within a selbri, indicating multiple inversions: a right-grouping rule is employed, as for 
{{vla|bo}}. The above rule can be applied to interpret such selbri, but all {{vla|co}} cmavo must be removed simultaneously:

:'''ckule co nixli co cmalu'''
:<code>school of-type (girl of-type little)</code>

becomes formally

:'''ke ke cmalu ke'e nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>( (little) girl ) school</code>

which by the left-grouping rule is simply

:'''cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>little girl school</code>
:''school for little girls''

As stated above, the selbri places, other than the first, of

:'''mi klama co sutra'''
:<code>I am-a-goer of-type quick</code>
:''I go quickly''

cannot be filled by placing sumti after the selbri, because any sumti in that position fill the places of {{vla|sutra}}, the seltau. However, the tertau places (which means in effect the selbri places) can be filled with {{vla|be}}:

:'''mi klama be le zarci be'o co sutra'''
:<code>I am-a-goer (to the store) of-type quick.</code>
:''I go to the store quickly.''

{{ssp|section-cmavo-selbri}}
==Other kinds of simple selbri==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|go'i}}
:{{s|GOhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|du}}
:{{s|GOhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|nu'a}}
:{{s|NUhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|moi}}
:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|mei}}
:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|nu}}
:{{s|NU}}
:''description''

:{{c|kei}}
:{{s|KEI}}
:''description''

So far we have only discussed brivla and tanru built up from brivla as possible selbri. In fact, there are a few other constructions in Lojban which are grammatically equivalent to brivla: they can be used either directly as selbri, or as components in tanru. Some of these types of simple selbri are discussed at length in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}, {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}, and {{lch|chapter-mekso}}; but for completeness these types are mentioned here with a brief explanation and an example of their use in selbri.

The cmavo of selma'o GOhA (with one exception) serve as pro-bridi, providing a reference to the content of other bridi; none of them has a fixed meaning. The most commonly used member of GOhA is probably {{vla|go'i}}, which amounts to a repetition of the previous bridi, or part of it. If I say:

:'''la djan. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John goes-to the market.</code>

you may retort:

:'''la djan. go'i troci'''
:<code>John [repeat last] are-a-tryer</code>
:''John tries to.''
{{lex|example-random-id-EvoD}} is short for:

:'''la djan. klama be le zarci be'o troci'''
:<code>John is-a-goer (to the market) type-of trier.</code>

because the whole bridi of {{lex|example-random-id-2UvG}} has been packaged up into the single word {{vla|go'i}} and inserted into {{lex|example-random-id-EvoD}}.

The exceptional member of GOhA is {{vla|du}}, which represents the relation of identity. Its place structure is:
:''x1 is identical with x2, x3, ...''
for as many places as are given. More information on selma'o GOhA is available in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}.

Lojban mathematical expressions (mekso) can be incorporated into selbri in two different ways. Mathematical operators such as 
{{vla|su'i}}, meaning “plus”, can be transformed into selbri by prefixing them with {{vla|nu'a}} (of selma'o NUhA). The resulting place structure is:
:''x1 is the result of applying (the operator) to arguments x2, x3, etc.''
for as many arguments as are required. (The result goes in the x1 place because the number of following places may be indefinite.) For example:

:'''li vo nu'a su'i li re li re'''
:<code>The-number 4 is-the-sum-of the-number 2 and-the-number 2.</code>

A possible tanru example might be:

:'''mi jimpe tu'a loi nu'a su'i nabmi'''
:<code>I understand something-about the-mass-of is-the-sum-of problems.</code>
:''I understand addition problems.''

More usefully, it is possible to combine a mathematical expression with a cmavo of selma'o MOI to create one of various numerical selbri. Details are available in 
{{ls|section-mekso-selbri}}. Here are a few tanru:

:'''la prim. palvr. pamoi cusku'''
:<code>Preem Palver is-the-1-th speaker.</code>
:''Preem Palver is the first speaker.''

:'''la an,iis. joi la .asun. bruna remei'''
:<code>Anyi massed-with Asun are-a-brother type-of-twosome.</code>
:''Anyi and Asun are two brothers.''

Finally, an important type of simple selbri which is not a brivla is the abstraction. Grammatically, abstractions are simple: a cmavo of selma'o NU, followed by a bridi, followed by the elidable terminator {{vla|kei}} of selma'o KEI. Semantically, abstractions are an extremely subtle and powerful feature of Lojban whose full ramifications are documented in {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}. A few examples:

:'''ti nu zdile kei kumfa'''
:<code>This is-an-event-of amusement room.</code>
:''This is an amusement room.''

{{lex|example-random-id-5szz}} is quite distinct in meaning from:

:'''ti zdile kumfa'''
:<code>This is-an-amuser room.</code>

which suggests the meaning “a room that amuses someone”.

{{ssp|section-me-selbri}}
==selbri based on sumti: {{vla|me}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|me}}
:{{s|ME}}
:''description''

:{{c|me'u}}
:{{s|MEhU}}
:''description''

A sumti can be made into a simple selbri by preceding it with {{vla|me}} (of selma'o ME) and following it with the elidable terminator {{vla|me'u}} (of selma'o MEhU). This makes a selbri with the place structure
:''x1 is one of the referents of “[the sumti]”''
which is true of the thing, or things, that are the referents of the sumti, and not of anything else. For example, consider the sumti

:'''le ci nolraitru'''
:<code>the three noblest-governors</code>
:''the three kings''

If these are understood to be the Three Kings of Christian tradition, who arrive every year on January 6, then we may say:

:'''la BALtazar. cu me le ci nolraitru'''
<code>Balthazar is one-of-the-referents-of “the three kings”.</code>
:''Balthazar is one of the three kings.''

and likewise

:'''la kaspar. cu me le ci nolraitru'''
:''Caspar is one of the three kings.''

and

:'''la melxi,or. cu me le ci nolraitru'''
:''Melchior is one of the three kings.''

If the sumti refers to a single object, then the effect of {{vla|me}} is much like that of {{vla|du}}:

:'''do du la djan.'''
:<code>You are-identical-with the-one-called “John”.</code>
:''You are John.''

means the same as

:'''do me la djan.'''
<code>You are-the-referent-of “the-one-called "John”".</code>
:''You are John.''

It is common to use {{vla|me}} selbri, especially those based on name sumti using {{vla|la}}, as seltau. For example:

:'''ta me lai kraislr. [me'u] karce'''
<code>That (is-a-referent of “the-mass-called "Chrysler"”) car.</code>
:''That is a Chrysler car.''

The elidable terminator {{vla|me'u}} can usually be omitted. It is absolutely required only if the {{vla|me}} selbri is being used in an indefinite description (a type of sumti explained in 
{{ls|section-indefinite-descriptions}}), and if the indefinite description is followed by a relative clause (explained in 
{{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}) or a sumti logical connective (explained in {{ls|section-sumti-connection}}). Without a {{vla|me'u}}, the relative clause or logical connective would appear to belong to the sumti embedded in the {{vla|me}} expression. Here is a contrasting pair of sentences:

:'''re me le ci nolraitru .e la djan. [me'u] cu blabi'''
:''Two of the group “the three kings and John” are white.''

:'''re me le ci nolraitru me'u .e la djan. cu blabi'''
:''Two of the three kings, and John, are white.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qJyi}} the {{vla|me}} selbri covers the three kings plus John, and the indefinite description picks out two of them that are said to be white: we cannot say which two. In {{lex|example-random-id-qJyK}}, though, the {{vla|me}} selbri covers only the three kings: two of them are said to be white, and so is John.

Finally, here is another example requiring {{vla|me'u}}:

:'''ta me la'e le se cusku be do me'u cukta'''
:<code>That is-a-(what-you-said) type of book.</code>
:''That is the kind of book you were talking about.''

There are other sentences where either {{vla|me'u}} or some other elidable terminator must be expressed:

:'''le me le ci nolraitru [ku] me'u nunsalci'''
:<code>the (the three kings) type-of-event-of-celebrating</code>
:''the Three Kings celebration''

requires either {{vla|ku}} or {{vla|me'u}} to be explicit, and (as with {{vla|be'o}} in {{ls|section-be-sumti}}) the {{vla|me'u}} leaves no doubt which cmavo it is paired with.

{{ssp|section-place-conversion}}
==Conversion of simple selbri==
Conversion is the process of changing a selbri so that its places appear in a different order. This is not the same as labeling the sumti with the cmavo of FA, as mentioned in {{ls|section-be-sumti}}, and then rearranging the order in which the sumti are spoken or written. Conversion transforms the selbri into a distinct, though closely related, selbri with renumbered places.

In Lojban, conversion is accomplished by placing a cmavo of selma'o SE before the selbri:

:'''mi prami do'''
:''I love you.''

is equivalent in meaning to:

:'''do se prami mi'''
:<code>You [swap x1 and x2] love me.</code>
:''You are loved by me.''

Conversion is fully explained in {{ls|section-SE}}. For the purposes of this chapter, the important point about conversion is that it applies only to the following simple selbri. When trying to convert a tanru, therefore, it is necessary to be careful! Consider {{lex|example-random-id-mPX8}}:

:'''la .alis. cu cadzu klama le zarci'''
:<code>Alice is-a-walker type-of goer to-the market.</code>
:<code>Alice walkingly goes to the market.</code>
:''Alice walks to the market.''

To convert this sentence so that 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} is in the x1 place, one correct way is:

:'''le zarci cu se ke cadzu klama [ke'e] la .alis.'''
:<code>The market is-a-[swap x1/x2] (walker type-of goer) Alice.</code>
:<code>The market is-walkingly gone-to by-Alice.</code>

The {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} brackets cause the entire tanru to be converted by the {{vla|se}}, which would otherwise convert only {{vla|cadzu}}, leading to:

:'''le zarci cu se cadzu klama la .alis.'''
:<code>The market (is-a-[swap x1/x2] walker) type-of goer to Alice.</code>
:<code>The market is-a-walking-surface type-of goer to Alice.</code>

whatever that might mean. An alternative approach, since the place structure of 
:{{jbo|cadzu klama}} is that of {{vla|klama}} alone, is to convert only the latter:

:'''le zarci cu cadzu se klama la .alis.'''
:<code>The market walkingly is-gone-to by-Alice.</code>

But the tanru in {{lex|example-random-id-U0fo}} may or may not have the same meaning as that in {{lex|example-random-id-mPX8}}; in particular, because {{vla|cadzu}} is not converted, there is a suggestion that although Alice is the goer, the market is the walker. With a different sumti as x1, this seemingly odd interpretation might make considerable sense:

:'''la djan. cu cadzu se klama la .alis'''
:<code>John walkingly is-gone-to by Alice</code>

suggests that Alice is going to John, who is a moving target.

There is an alternative type of conversion, using the cmavo {{vla|jai}} of selma'o JAI optionally followed by a modal or tense construction. Grammatically, such a combination behaves exactly like conversion using SE. More details can be found in {{ls|section-modal-jai}}.

{{ssp|section-selbri-scalar-negation}}
==Scalar negation of selbri==
Negation is too large and complex a topic to explain fully in this chapter; See {{lch|chapter-negation}}. In brief, there are two main types of negation in Lojban. This section is concerned with so-called “scalar negation”, which is used to state that a true relation between the sumti is something other than what the selbri specifies. Scalar negation is expressed by cmavo of selma'o NAhE:

:'''la .alis. cu na'e ke cadzu klama [ke'e] le zarci'''
:<code>Alice non- (walkingly goes) to-the market.</code>
:<code>Alice other-than (walkingly goes) to-the market.</code>
:''Alice doesn't walk to the market.''

meaning that Alice's relationship to the market is something other than that of walking there. But if the {{vla|ke}} were omitted, the result would be:

:'''la .alis. cu na'e cadzu klama le zarci'''
:<code>Alice non- walkingly goes to-the market.</code>
:''Alice doesn't walk to the market.''

meaning that Alice does go there in some way ( {{vla|klama}} is not negated), but by a means other than that of walking. {{lex|example-random-id-4oxH}} negates both {{vla|cadzu}} and {{vla|klama}}, suggesting that Alice's relation to the market is something different from walkingly-going; it might be walking without going, or going without walking, or neither.

Of course, any of the simple selbri types explained in {{ls|section-cmavo-selbri}} may be used in place of brivla in any of these examples:

:'''la djonz. cu na'e pamoi cusku'''
:<code>Jones is non-1st speaker</code>
:''Jones is not the first speaker.''

Since only {{vla|pamoi}} is negated, an appropriate inference is that he is some other kind of speaker.

Here is an assortment of more complex examples showing the interaction of scalar negation with {{vla|bo}} grouping, {{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}} grouping, logical connection, and sumti linked with {{vla|be}} and {{vla|bei}}:

:'''mi na'e sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o klama le zarci'''
:<code>I ( (non-quickly) ( walking using the arms) ) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, walking using my arms other than quickly.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-I1Rd}}, {{vla|na'e}} negates only {{vla|sutra}}. Contrast {{lex|example-random-id-KcK8}}:

:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka [be'o] ke'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I non- ( quickly (walking using the arms) ) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, other than by walking quickly on my arms.''

Now consider {{lex|example-random-id-qjyW}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjyy}}, which are equivalent in meaning, but use {{vla|ke}} grouping and {{vla|bo}} grouping respectively:

:'''mi sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I (quickly &ndash; (walking using the arms) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both quickly walking using my arms and slowly.''

:'''mi ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka [be'o] ke'e je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I ( (quickly (walking using the arms) ) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both quickly walking using my arms and slowly.''

However, if we place a {{vla|na'e}} at the beginning of the selbri in both {{lex|example-random-id-qjyW}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjyy}}, we get different results:

:'''mi na'e sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I ( (non- quickly) - (walking using the arms) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both walking using my arms other than quickly, and also slowly.''

:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka [be'o] ke'e je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I (non-(quickly (walking using the arms) ) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both other than quickly walking using my arms, and also slowly.''

The difference arises because the {{vla|na'e}} in {{lex|example-random-id-qJzr}} negates the whole construction from {{vla|ke}} to {{vla|ke'e}}, whereas in {{lex|example-random-id-qjyz}} it negates {{vla|sutra}} alone.

Beware of omitting terminators in these complex examples! If the explicit 
{{vla|ke'e}} is left out in {{lex|example-random-id-qJzr}}, it is transformed into:

:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o je masno klama [ke'e] le zarci'''
:<code>I non-(quickly ( (walking using the arms) ) and slowly) go-to) the market.</code>
:<code>I do something other than quickly both going to the market walking</code>
:''using my arms and slowly going to the market.''

And if both {{vla|ke'e}} and {{vla|be'o}} are omitted, the results are even sillier:

:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka je masno klama [be'o] [ke'e] le zarci'''
:<code>I non-(quickly walk on my (arm-type and slow) goers) on the market.</code>
:''I do something other than quickly walking using the goers, both arm-type and slow, relative-to the market.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-0WLq}}, everything after {{vla|be}} is a linked sumti, so the place structure is that of 
{{vla|cadzu}}, whose x2 place is the surface walked upon. It is less than clear what an “arm-type goer” might be. Furthermore, since the x3 place has been occupied by the linked sumti, the 

:{{jbo|le zarci}} following the selbri falls into the nonexistent x4 place of {{vla|cadzu}}. As a result, the whole example, though grammatical, is complete nonsense. (The bracketed Lojban words appear where a fluent Lojbanist would understand them to be implied.)

Finally, it is also possible to place {{vla|na'e}} before a {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} logically connected tanru construction. The meaning of this usage has not yet been firmly established.

{{ssp|section-bridi-negation-tenses}}
==Tenses and bridi negation==
A bridi can have cmavo associated with it which specify the time, place, or mode of action. For example, in

:'''mi pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [past] go to-the market.</code>
:''I went to the market.''

the cmavo {{vla|pu}} specifies that the action of the speaker going to the market takes place in the past. Tenses are explained in full detail in {{lch|chapter-tenses}}. Tense is semantically a property of the entire bridi; however, the usual syntax for tenses attaches them at the front of the selbri, as in {{lex|example-random-id-uz13}}. There are alternative ways of expressing tense information as well. Modals, which are explained in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}}, behave in the same way as tenses.

Similarly, a bridi may have the particle {{vla|na}} (of selma'o NA) attached to the beginning of the selbri to negate the bridi. A negated bridi expresses what is false without saying anything about what is true. Do not confuse this usage with the scalar negation of {{ls|section-selbri-scalar-negation}}. For example:

:'''la djonz. na pamoi cusku'''
:<code>Jones (Not!) is-the-first speaker</code>
:<code>It is not true that Jones is the first speaker.</code>
:''Jones isn't the first speaker.''

Jones may be the second speaker, or not a speaker at all; {{lex|example-random-id-PYSP}} doesn't say. There are other ways of expressing bridi negation as well; the topic is explained fully in {{lch|chapter-negation}}.

Various combinations of tense and bridi negation cmavo are permitted. If both are expressed, either order is permissible with no change in meaning:

:'''mi na pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>mi pu na klama le zarci</code>
:<code>It is false that I went to the market.</code>
:''I didn't go to the market.''

It is also possible to have more than one {{vla|na}}, in which case pairs of {{vla|na}} cmavo cancel out:

:'''mi na na klama le zarci'''
:<code>It is false that it is false that I go to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market.''

It is even possible, though somewhat pointless, to have multiple {{vla|na}} cmavo and tense cmavo mixed together, subject to the limitation that two adjacent tense cmavo will be understood as a compound tense, and must fit the grammar of tenses as explained in 
{{lch|chapter-tenses}}.

:'''mi na pu na ca klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [not] [past] [not] [present] go to-the market</code>
:<code>It is not the case that in the past it was not the case that in the present I went to the market.</code>
:<code>I didn't not go to the market.</code>
:''I went to the market.''

Tense, modal, and negation cmavo can appear only at the beginning of the selbri. They cannot be embedded within it.

{{ssp|section-asymmetric-tanru}}
==Some types of asymmetrical tanru==

This section and {{ls|section-symmetric-tanru}} contain some example tanru classified into groups based on the type of relationship between the modifying seltau and the modified tertau. All the examples are paralleled by compounds actually observed in various natural languages. In the tables which follow, each group is preceded by a brief explanation of the relationship. The tables themselves contain a tanru, a literal gloss, an indication of the languages which exhibit a compound analogous to this tanru, and (for those tanru with no English parallel) a translation.

Here are the 3-letter abbreviations used for the various languages (it is presumed to be obvious whether a compound is found in English or not, so English is not explicitly noted):

;'''Aba'''
:Abazin

;'''Chi'''
:Chinese

;'''Ewe'''
:Ewe

;'''Fin'''
:Finnish

;'''Geo'''
:Georgian

;'''Gua'''
:Guarani

;'''Hop'''
:Hopi

;'''Hun'''
:Hungarian

;'''Imb'''
:Imbabura Quechua

;'''Kar'''
:Karaitic

;'''Kaz'''
:Kazakh

;'''Kor'''
:Korean

;'''Mon'''
:Mongolian

;'''Qab'''
:Qabardian

;'''Que'''
:Quechua

;'''Rus'''
:Russian

;'''Skt'''
:Sanskrit

;'''Swe'''
:Swedish

;'''Tur'''
:Turkish

;'''Udm'''
:Udmurt

Any lujvo or fu'ivla used in a group are glossed at the end of that group.

The tanru discussed in this section are asymmetrical tanru; that is, ones in which the order of the terms is fundamental to the meaning of the tanru. For example, 

:{{jbo|junla dadysli}}, or “clock pendulum”, is the kind of pendulum used in a clock, whereas 
:{{jbo|dadysli junla}}, or “pendulum clock”, is the kind of clock that employs a pendulum. Most tanru are asymmetrical in this sense. Symmetrical tanru are discussed in {{ls|section-symmetric-tanru}}.

The tertau represents an action, and the seltau then represents the object of that action:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>{{jbo|pinsi nunkilbra}}	pencil sharpener	Hun
{{jbo|zgike nunctu}}	music instruction	Hun
{{jbo|mirli nunkalte}}	deer hunting	Hun
{{jbo|finpe nunkalte}}	fish hunting	Tur,Kor,Udm,Aba	fishing
{{jbo|smacu terkavbu}}	mousetrap	Tur,Kor,Hun,Udm,Aba
{{jbo|zdani turni}}	house ruler	Kar	host
{{jbo|zerle'a nunte'a}}	thief fear	Skt	fear of thieves
{{jbo|cevni zekri}}	god crime	Skt	offense against the gods
</tab>

;{{vla|nunkilbra}}
:sharpness-apparatus

;{{vla|nunctu}}
:event-of-teaching

;{{vla|nunkalte}}
:event-of-hunting

;{{vla|terkavbu}}
:trap

;{{vla|zerle'a}}
:crime-taker

;{{vla|nunte'a}}
:event-of-fearing

The tertau represents a set, and the seltau the type of the elements contained in that set:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|zdani lijgri}}	house row
{{jbo|selci lamgri}}	cell block
{{jbo|karda mulgri}}	card pack	Swe
{{jbo|rokci derxi}}	stone heap	Swe
{{jbo|tadni girzu}}	student group	Hun
{{jbo|remna girzu}}	human-being group	Qab	group of people
{{jbo|cpumi'i lijgri}}	tractor column	Qab
{{jbo|cevni jenmi}}	god army	Skt
{{jbo|cevni prenu}}	god folk	Skt
</tab>

;{{vla|lijgri}}
:line-group

;{{vla|lamgri}}
:adjacent-group

;{{vla|mulgri}}
:complete-group

;{{vla|cpumi'i}}
:pull-machine

Conversely: the tertau is an element, and the seltau represents a set in which that element is contained. Implicitly, the meaning of the tertau is restricted from its usual general meaning to the specific meaning appropriate for elements in the given set. Note the opposition between 
:{{jbo|zdani linji}} in the previous group, and 
:{{jbo|linji zdani}} in this one, which shows why this kind of tanru is called “asymmetrical”.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|carvi dirgo}}	raindrop	Tur,Kor,Hun,Udm,Aba
{{jbo|linji zdani}}	row house
</tab>
The seltau specifies an object and the tertau a component or detail of that object; the tanru as a whole refers to the detail, specifying that it is a detail of that whole and not some other.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|junla dadysli}}	clock pendulum	Hun
{{jbo|purdi vorme}}	garden door	Qab
{{jbo|purdi bitmu}}	garden wall	Que
{{jbo|moklu skapi}}	mouth skin	Imb	lips
{{jbo|nazbi kevna}}	nose hole	Imb	nostril
{{jbo|karce xislu}}	automobile wheel	Chi
{{jbo|jipci pimlu}}	chicken feather	Chi
{{jbo|vinji rebla}}	airplane tail	Chi
</tab>

;{{vla|dadysli}}
:hang-oscillator

Conversely: the seltau specifies a characteristic or important detail of the object described by the tertau; objects described by the tanru as a whole are differentiated from other similar objects by this detail.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|pixra cukta}}	picture book
{{jbo|kerfa silka}}	hair silk	Kar	velvet
{{jbo|plise tapla}}	apple cake	Tur
{{jbo|dadysli junla}}	pendulum clock	Hun
</tab>
;{{vla|dadysli}}
:hang-oscillator

The tertau specifies a general class of object (a genus), and the seltau specifies a sub-class of that class (a species):
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|ckunu tricu}}	pine tree	Hun,Tur,Hop
</tab>
The tertau specifies an object of possession, and the seltau may specify the possessor (the possession may be intrinsic or otherwise). In English, these compounds have an explicit possessive element in them: “lion's mane”, “child's foot”, “noble's cow”.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cinfo kerfa}}	lion mane	Kor,Tur,Hun,Udm,Qab
{{jbo|verba jamfu}}	child foot	Swe
{{jbo|nixli tuple}}	girl leg	Swe
{{jbo|cinfo jamfu}}	lion foot	Que
{{jbo|danlu skapi}}	animal skin	Ewe
{{jbo|ralju zdani}}	chief house	Ewe
{{jbo|jmive munje}}	living world	Skt
{{jbo|nobli bakni}}	noble cow	Skt
{{jbo|nolraitru ralju}}	king chief	Skt	emperor
</tab>

;{{vla|nolraitru}}
:nobly-superlative-ruler

The tertau specifies a habitat, and the seltau specifies the inhabitant:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|lanzu tumla}}	family land
</tab>
The tertau specifies a causative agent, and the seltau specifies the effect of that cause:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kalselvi'i gapci}}	tear gas	Hun
{{jbo|terbi'a jurme}}	disease germ	Tur
{{jbo|fenki litki}}	crazy liquid	Hop	whisky
{{jbo|pinca litki}}	urine liquid	Hop	beer
</tab>

;{{vla|kalselvi'i}}
:eye-excreted-thing

;{{vla|terbi'a}}
:disease

Conversely: the tertau specifies an effect, and the seltau specifies its cause.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|djacu barna}}	water mark	Chi
</tab>
The tertau specifies an instrument, and the seltau specifies the purpose of that instrument:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|taxfu dadgreku}}	garment rack	Chi
{{jbo|tergu'i ti'otci}}	lamp shade	Chi
{{jbo|xirma zdani}}	horse house	Chi	stall
{{jbo|nuzba tanbo}}	news board	Chi	bulletin board
</tab>

;{{vla|dadgreku}}
:hang-frame

;{{vla|tergu'i}}
:source of illumination

;{{vla|ti'otci}}
:shadow-tool

More vaguely: the tertau specifies an instrument, and the seltau specifies the object of the purpose for which that instrument is used:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cpina rokci}}	pepper stone	Que	stone for grinding pepper
{{jbo|jamfu djacu}}	foot water	Skt	water for washing the feet
{{jbo|grana mudri}}	post wood	Skt	wood for making a post
{{jbo|moklu djacu}}	mouth water	Hun	water for washing the mouth
{{jbo|lanme gerku}}	sheep dog		dog for working sheep
</tab>
The tertau specifies a product from some source, and the seltau specifies the source of the product:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|moklu djacu}}	mouth water	Aba,Qab	saliva
{{jbo|ractu mapku}}	rabbit hat	Rus
{{jbo|jipci sovda}}	chicken egg	Chi
{{jbo|sikcurnu silka}}	silkworm silk	Chi
{{jbo|mlatu kalci}}	cat feces	Chi
{{jbo|bifce lakse}}	bee wax	Chi	beeswax
{{jbo|cribe rectu}}	bear meat	Tur,Kor,Hun,Udm,Aba
{{jbo|solxrula grasu}}	sunflower oil	Tur,Kor,Hun,Udm,Aba
{{jbo|bifce jisra}}	bee juice	Hop	honey
{{jbo|tatru litki}}	breast liquid	Hop	milk
{{jbo|kanla djacu}}	eye water	Kor	tear
</tab>

;{{vla|sikcurnu}}
:silk-worm

;{{vla|solxrula}}
:solar-flower

Conversely: the tertau specifies the source of a product, and the seltau specifies the product:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|silna jinto}}	salt well	Chi
{{jbo|kolme terkakpa}}	coal mine	Chi
{{jbo|ctile jinto}}	oil well	Chi
</tab>

;{{vla|terkakpa}}
:source of digging

The tertau specifies an object, and the seltau specifies the material from which the object is made. This case is especially interesting, because the referent of the tertau may normally be made from just one kind of material, which is then overridden in the tanru.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|rokci cinfo}}	stone lion
{{jbo|snime nanmu}}	snow man	Hun
{{jbo|kliti cipni}}	clay bird
{{jbo|blaci kanla}}	glass eye	Hun
{{jbo|blaci kanla}}	glass eye	Que	spectacles
{{jbo|solji sicni}}	gold coin	Tur
{{jbo|solji junla}}	gold watch	Tur,Kor,Hun
{{jbo|solji djine}}	gold ring	Udm,Aba,Que
{{jbo|rokci zdani}}	stone house	Imb
{{jbo|mudri zdani}}	wood house	Ewe	wooden house
{{jbo|rokci bitmu}}	stone wall	Ewe
{{jbo|solji carce}}	gold chariot	Skt
{{jbo|mudri xarci}}	wood weapon	Skt	wooden weapon
{{jbo|cmaro'i dargu}}	pebble road	Chi
{{jbo|sudysrasu cutci}}	straw shoe	Chi
</tab>

;{{vla|cmaro'i}}
:small-rock

;{{vla|sudysrasu}}
:dry-grass

Note: the two senses of 
:{{jbo|blaci kanla}} can be discriminated as:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|blaci kanla bo tarmi}}	glass (eye shape)	glass eye
{{jbo|blaci kanla bo sidju}}	glass (eye helper)	spectacles
</tab>
The tertau specifies a typical object used to measure a quantity and the seltau specifies something measured. The tanru as a whole refers to a given quantity of the thing being measured. English does not have compounds of this form, as a rule.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|tumla spisa}}	land piece	Tur	piece of land
{{jbo|tcati kabri}}	tea cup	Kor,Aba	cup of tea
{{jbo|nanba spisa}}	bread piece	Kor	piece of bread
{{jbo|bukpu spisa}}	cloth piece	Udm,Aba	piece of cloth
{{jbo|djacu calkyguzme}}	water calabash	Ewe	calabash of water
</tab>

;{{vla|calkyguzme}}
:shell-fruit, calabash

The tertau specifies an object with certain implicit properties, and the seltau overrides one of those implicit properties:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kensa bloti}}	spaceship
{{jbo|bakni verba}}	cattle child	Ewe	calf
</tab>
The seltau specifies a whole, and the tertau specifies a part which normally is associated with a different whole. The tanru then refers to a part of the seltau which stands in the same relationship to the whole seltau as the tertau stands to its typical whole.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kosta degji}}	coat finger	Hun	coat sleeve
{{jbo|denci genja}}	tooth root	Imb
{{jbo|tricu stedu}}	tree head	Imb	treetop
</tab>
The tertau specifies the producer of a certain product, and the seltau specifies the product. In this way, the tanru as a whole distinguishes its referents from other referents of the tertau which do not produce the product.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|silka curnu}}	silkworm	Tur,Hun,Aba
</tab>
The tertau specifies an object, and the seltau specifies another object which has a characteristic property. The tanru as a whole refers to those referents of the tertau which possess the property.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|sonci manti}}	soldier ant
{{jbo|ninmu bakni}}	woman cattle	Imb	cow
{{jbo|mamta degji}}	mother finger	Imb	thumb
{{jbo|cifnu degji}}	baby finger	Imb	pinky
{{jbo|pacraistu zdani}}	hell house	Skt
{{jbo|fagri dapma}}	fire curse	Skt	curse destructive as fire
</tab>

;{{vla|pacraistu}}
:evil-superlative-site

As a particular case (when the property is that of resemblance): the seltau specifies an object which the referent of the tanru resembles.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|grutrceraso jbama}}	cherry bomb
{{jbo|solji kerfa}}	gold hair	Hun	golden hair
{{jbo|kanla djacu}}	eye water	Kar	spring
{{jbo|bakni rokci}}	bull stone	Mon	boulder
</tab>

;{{vla|grutrceraso}}
:fu'ivla for “cherry” based on Linnean name

The seltau specifies a place, and the tertau an object characteristically located in or at that place.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|ckana boxfo}}	bed sheet	Chi
{{jbo|mrostu mojysu'a}}	tomb monument	Chi	tombstone
{{jbo|jubme tergusni}}	table lamp	Chi
{{jbo|foldi smacu}}	field mouse	Chi
{{jbo|briju ci'ajbu}}	office desk	Chi
{{jbo|rirxe xirma}}	river horse	Chi	hippopotamus
{{jbo|xamsi gerku}}	sea dog	Chi	seal
{{jbo|cagyce'u zdani}}	village house	Skt
</tab>

;{{vla|mrostu}}
:dead-site

;{{vla|mojysu'a}}
:remember-structure

;{{vla|ci'ajbu}}
:write-table

;{{vla|cagyce'u}}
:farm-community

Specifically: the tertau is a place where the seltau is sold or made available to the public.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cidja barja}}	food bar	Chi	restaurant
{{jbo|cukta barja}}	book bar	Chi	library
</tab>
The seltau specifies the locus of application of the tertau.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kanla velmikce}}	eye medicine	Chi
{{jbo|jgalu grasu}}	nail oil	Chi	nail polish
{{jbo|denci pesxu}}	tooth paste	Chi
</tab>

;{{vla|velmikce}}
:treatment used by doctor

The tertau specifies an implement used in the activity denoted by the seltau.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|me la pinpan. bolci}}	Ping-Pong ball	Chi
</tab>
The tertau specifies a protective device against the undesirable features of the referent of the seltau.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|carvi mapku}}	rain cap	Chi
{{jbo|carvi taxfu}}	rain garment	Chi	raincoat
{{jbo|vindu firgai}}	poison mask	Chi	gas mask
</tab>

;{{vla|firgai}}
:face-cover

The tertau specifies a container characteristically used to hold the referent of the seltau.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cukta vasru}}	book vessel	Chi	satchel
{{jbo|vanju kabri}}	wine cup	Chi
{{jbo|spatrkoka lanka}}	coca basket	Que
{{jbo|rismi dakli}}	rice bag	Ewe,Chi
{{jbo|tcati kabri}}	tea cup	Chi

{{jbo|cladakyxa'i zdani}}	sword house	Kor	sheath
{{jbo|manti zdani}}	ant nest	Gua	anthill
</tab>

;{{vla|spatrkoka}}

;{{vla|cladakyxa'i}}

The seltau specifies the characteristic time of the event specified by the tertau.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|vensa djedi}}	spring day	Chi

</tab>
The seltau specifies a source of energy for the referent of the tertau.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|dikca tergusni}}	electric lamp	Chi

</tab>

;{{vla|tergusni}}

Finally, some tanru which don't fall into any of the above categories.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|ladru denci}}	milk tooth	Tur,Hun,Udm,Qab
{{jbo|kanla denci}}	eye tooth
</tab>
It is clear that “tooth” is being specified, and that “milk” and “eye” act as modifiers. However, the relationship between {{vla|ladru}} and {{vla|denci}} is something like “tooth which one has when one is drinking milk from one's mother”, a relationship certainly present nowhere except in this particular concept. As for 
:{{jbo|kanla denci}}, the relationship is not only not present on the surface, it is hardly possible to formulate it at all.

{{ssp|section-symmetric-tanru}}
==Some types of symmetrical tanru==

This section deals with symmetrical tanru, where order is not important. Many of these tanru can be expressed with a logical or non-logical connective between the components.

The tanru may refer to things which are correctly specified by both tanru components. Some of these instances may also be seen as asymmetrical tanru where the seltau specifies a material. The connective 
{{vla|je}} is appropriate:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cipnrstrigi pacru'i}}	owl demon	Skt
{{jbo|nolraitru prije}}	royal sage	Skt
{{jbo|remna nakni}}	human-being male	Qab	man
{{jbo|remna fetsi}}	human-being female	Qab	woman
{{jbo|sonci tolvri}}	soldier coward	Que
{{jbo|panzi nanmu}}	offspring man	Ewe	son
{{jbo|panzi ninmu}}	offspring woman	Ewe	daughter
{{jbo|solji sicni}}	gold coin	Tur
{{jbo|solji junla}}	gold watch	Tur,Kor,Hun
{{jbo|solji djine}}	gold ring	Udm,Aba,Que

{{ssp|section-pretty-school-groupings}}
==“Pretty little girls' school”: forty ways to say it==
The following examples show every possible grouping arrangement of 
:{{jbo|melbi cmalu nixli ckule}} using {{vla|bo}} or {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} for grouping and {{vla|je}} or {{vla|je}}{{vla|bo}} for logical connection. Most of these are definitely not plausible interpretations of the English phrase “pretty little girls' school”, especially those which describe something which is both a girl and a school.

Examples {{lex|example-random-id-qjmr}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qjNi}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qjog}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-tz0L}} are repeated here as Examples {{lex|example-random-id-qjzw}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKaM}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKfX}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKmg}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-qKPQ}} respectively.
<!-- was: Examples 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, and 5.6 are repeated here as Examples 16.1, 16.9, 16.17, 16.25, and 16.33 respectively. -->
The seven examples following each of these share the same grouping pattern, but differ in the presence or absence of {{vla|je}} at each possible site. Some of the examples have more than one Lojban version. In that case, they differ only in grouping mechanism, and are always equivalent in meaning.

The logical connective {{vla|je}} is associative: that is, “A and (B and C)” is the same as “(A and B) and C”. Therefore, some of the examples have the same meaning as others. In particular, {{lex|example-random-id-qKAG}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKFA}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKLN}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKpo}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-qKU6}} all have the same meaning because all four brivla are logically connected and the grouping is simply irrelevant.
<!-- was: In particular, 16.8, 16.16, 16.24, 16.32, and 16.40 all have the same meaning -->
Other equivalent forms are noted in the examples themselves. However, if 
{{vla|je}} were replaced by {{vla|naja}} or {{vla|jo}} or most of the other logical connectives, the meanings would become distinct.

It must be emphasized that, because of the ambiguity of all tanru, the English translations are by no means definitive &ndash; they represent only one possible interpretation of the corresponding Lojban sentence.

:'''melbi cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>((pretty type-of little) type-of girl) type-of school</code>
:''school for girls who are beautifully small''

:'''melbi je cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>((pretty and little) type-of girl) type-of school</code>
:''school for girls who are beautiful and small''

:'''melbi bo cmalu je nixli ckule'''
:<code>((pretty type-of little) and girl) type-of school</code>
:''school for girls and for beautifully small things''

:'''ke melbi cmalu nixli ke'e je ckule'''
:<code>((pretty type-of little) type-of girl) and school</code>
:''thing which is a school and a beautifully small girl''

:'''melbi je cmalu je nixli ckule'''
:<code>((pretty and little) and girl) type-of school</code>
:<code>school for things which are beautiful, small, and girls</code>
Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qKjr}}

:'''melbi bo cmalu je nixli je ckule'''
:<code>((pretty type-of little) and girl) and school</code>
:<code>thing which is beautifully small, a school, and a girl</code>
Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qKdY}}

:'''ke melbi je cmalu nixli ke'e je ckule'''
:<code>((pretty and little) type-of girl) and school</code>
:''thing which is a school and a girl who is both beautiful and small''

:'''melbi je cmalu je nixli je ckule'''
:<code>((pretty and little) and girl) and school</code>
:''thing which is beautiful, small, a girl, and a school''

:'''melbi cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of little) type-of (girl type-of school)</code>
:''girls' school which is beautifully small''

:'''melbi je cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and little) type-of (girl type-of school)</code>
:''girls' school which is beautiful and small''

:'''melbi cmalu nixli je ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of little) type-of (girl and school)</code>
:''something which is a girl and a school which is beautifully small''

:'''melbi bo cmalu je nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of little) and (girl type-of school)</code>
:''something which is beautifully small and a girls' school''

:'''melbi je cmalu nixli je ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and little) type-of (girl and school)</code>
:''a pretty and little type of thing which is both a girl and a school''

:'''melbi bo cmalu je nixli jebo ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of little) and (girl and school)</code>
:''thing which is beautifully small, a school, and a girl''

Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qK7I}}

:'''melbi jebo cmalu je nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and little) and (girl type-of school)</code>
:''thing which is beautiful and small and a girl's school''

Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qKpm}}

:'''melbi jebo cmalu je nixli jebo ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and little) and (girl and school)</code>
:''thing which is beautiful, small, a girl, and a school''

:'''melbi cmalu bo nixli ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of (little type-of girl)) type-of school</code>
:''school for beautiful girls who are small''

:'''melbi cmalu je nixli ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of (little and girl)) type-of school</code>
:''school for beautiful things which are small and are girls''

:'''melbi je cmalu bo nixli ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and (little type-of girl)) type-of school</code>
:''school for things which are beautiful and are small girls''

:'''ke melbi cmalu bo nixli ke'e je ckule'''
:'''melbi bo cmalu bo nixli je ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of (little type-of girl)) and school</code>
:''thing which is a school and a small girl who is beautiful''

:'''melbi je cmalu jebo nixli ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and (little and girl)) type-of school</code>
:''school for things which are beautiful, small, and girls''

Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qK5Y}}

:'''melbi je cmalu bo nixli je ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and (little type-of girl)) and school</code>
:''thing which is beautiful, a small girl, and a school''

Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qKsA}}

:'''ke melbi cmalu je nixli ke'e je ckule'''
:<code>(pretty type-of (little and girl)) and school</code>
:''thing which is beautifully small, a beautiful girl, and a school''

:'''melbi je cmalu jebo nixli je ckule'''
:<code>(pretty and (little and girl)) and school</code>
:''thing which is beautiful, small, a girl, and a school''

:'''melbi cmalu bo nixli bo ckule'''
:'''melbi ke cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e] [ke'e]'''

:'''melbi ke cmalu nixli je ckule [ke'e]'''

:'''melbi cmalu je nixli bo ckule'''

:'''melbi je cmalu bo nixli bo ckule'''
:'''melbi je ke cmalu nixli bo ckule [ke'e]'''

Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qKR5}}

Note: same as {{lex|example-random-id-qKEI}}
